lanes.label: Elsewhere in scripture
lanes.range: Topics in other books wired to this one

nodes.d: Leviticus gives the LORD's instructions from the tabernacle: the offerings, the consecration of the priests, clean and unclean, the day of atonement, holy living, the feasts, the jubilee, and the blessings and curses of obedience.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} give a one-sentence summary of what Leviticus is about?
ev: Name the main sections of Leviticus (offerings, priests, clean and unclean, atonement, holiness, feasts, jubilee, blessings and curses).

nodes.d: Leviticus 1 describes the burnt offering from the herd, flock or birds: an unblemished male brought to the tabernacle door, a hand laid on its head so that it is accepted to make atonement, and all of it burned on the altar.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the burnt offering was and why the animal had to be without blemish?
ev: Describe what the worshipper and the priests each did with the burnt offering.
Say what verse 4 says the laid-on hand and the offering accomplish.

nodes.d: Leviticus 2 describes the grain (meat) offering of fine flour with oil and frankincense, a memorial portion burned and the rest given to the priests, with no leaven or honey and salt on every offering.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} describe the grain offering and say what happened to the part that was not burned?
ev: List what went into a grain offering and what was kept out of it.
Say who received the part that was not burned.

nodes.d: Leviticus 3 describes the peace offering from herd or flock, male or female, without blemish: hand laid on the head, blood sprinkled, the fat burned on the altar, with a lasting rule against eating fat or blood.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain how the peace offering differs from the burnt offering in what is burned?
ev: Say what part of the peace offering was burned and what was forbidden to eat (3:17).

nodes.d: Leviticus 4 gives the sin offering for sins done through ignorance, with different procedures for the anointed priest, the whole congregation, a ruler and a common person, each ending in atonement and forgiveness.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain who the sin offering was for and what the text says it achieves (for example 4:20, 26)?
ev: Name the four groups of people in chapter 4 and the animal each brings.
Say where the blood was put in the case of the priest and the congregation.

nodes.d: Leviticus 5:1-6:7 lists wrongs needing a trespass offering (silence as a witness, uncleanness, rash oaths, trespass in holy things, deceit toward a neighbour), with confession, a graded offering by ability, and restitution plus a fifth.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why restitution is required alongside the trespass offering?
ev: State what the guilty person must do besides bringing an offering (confess, restore, add a fifth).
Describe how the offering changes if he cannot afford a lamb.

nodes.t: The priests' laws of the offerings
nodes.d: Leviticus 6:8-7:38 gives the priests' instructions for the burnt, grain, sin, trespass and peace offerings: the fire never to go out, which portions the priests eat, and the rules on fat, blood and the wave breast and heave shoulder.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the priests received from the offerings?
ev: Say what was to be kept burning continually on the altar.
Name which offerings the priests ate and which portion went to them from the peace offerings.

nodes.t: Aaron and his sons are consecrated
nodes.d: Leviticus 8 records Moses washing, clothing and anointing Aaron and his sons, anointing the tabernacle, and the sin, burnt and consecration offerings over seven days, as the LORD commanded.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell how Aaron and his sons were set apart as priests?
ev: Retell the order of events in the consecration of Aaron and his sons.
Find the phrase showing that they did as the LORD commanded (8:36).

nodes.t: The eighth day: glory and fire
nodes.d: Leviticus 9 tells how on the eighth day Aaron offered for himself and the people, blessed them, and the glory of the LORD appeared as fire came out and consumed the offering, so that the people shouted and fell on their faces.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell what happened on the eighth day and how the people responded?
ev: Say what Aaron offered first and why, then what he offered for the people.
Describe what happened at the end of the chapter (9:23-24).

nodes.d: Leviticus 10 tells how Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu offered fire before the LORD, fire came out and killed them, and Moses and Aaron respond; the chapter adds a rule about wine for priests and a question over the sin offering.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the death of Nadab and Abihu teaches about approaching the LORD?
ev: Tell what Nadab and Abihu did and what happened.
State what Moses said the LORD means by being sanctified in those who come near (10:3).

nodes.d: Leviticus 11 distinguishes animals that may and may not be eaten (land animals, water creatures, birds, insects) and what contact with carcasses makes one unclean, closing with the call to be holy because the LORD is holy.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain the reason the chapter itself gives for the clean and unclean laws?
ev: Give the two marks of a land animal that may be eaten (11:3) and one animal that fails them.
Find the reason given in 11:44-45 for these laws.

nodes.d: Leviticus 12 sets the days of uncleanness after the birth of a son or daughter, circumcision on the eighth day, and the lamb and bird (or two birds if poor) offered for her cleansing.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} describe what a woman did at the end of the days of purifying?
ev: State when a boy is to be circumcised according to 12:3.
Say what offerings she brings and what changes if she cannot afford a lamb.

nodes.t: Diseases of skin, clothing and houses
nodes.d: Leviticus 13 describes how the priest examines skin diseases, with seven-day confinement, pronouncing clean or unclean, the separation of the unclean person outside the camp, and a similar examination of diseased garments.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain who decided whether someone was clean and what happened to an unclean person?
ev: Say who judges whether a person is clean or unclean and what steps he takes.
Describe what the person with the disease must do (13:45-46).

nodes.t: Cleansing from disease and from mould
nodes.d: Leviticus 14 gives the rite for cleansing a healed person (two birds, cedar, scarlet, hyssop, washing, then offerings on the eighth day with blood and oil) and the examination and cleansing of a house with spreading plague.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} describe how a healed person was declared clean again?
ev: Describe the two stages of the cleansing rite (day of cleansing and eighth day).
Say what the priest does to a house with a plague.

nodes.d: Leviticus 15 deals with uncleanness from bodily discharges of men and women, how it spreads to beds and things touched, washing and waiting seven days, and the sin and burnt offerings on the eighth day.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why the text says Israel is to be kept separate from uncleanness (15:31)?
ev: Say what a person must do to be clean after a discharge ends (seven days, washing, two birds on the eighth day).
Find the reason given in 15:31 for these separations.

nodes.d: Leviticus 16 sets out how, after Nadab and Abihu died, Aaron enters the holy place once a year with offerings for himself and the people, blood on the mercy seat, and a live goat that carries the people's iniquities into the wilderness.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what happened on the day of atonement and what the two goats show?
ev: Explain why Aaron must not come into the holy place at just any time (16:2).
Describe the two goats and what happens to each.
State the date and the people's duty on that day (16:29-31).

nodes.t: Sacrifices at the door and the sanctity of blood
nodes.d: Leviticus 17 requires that sacrifices be brought to the tabernacle door rather than offered in the open fields, and forbids eating blood, because the life of the flesh is in the blood which the LORD gave on the altar to make atonement.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why blood was treated as special according to Leviticus 17:11?
ev: State the reason given in 17:11 for the ban on eating blood.
Say what had to be done with blood from an animal taken in hunting (17:13).

nodes.t: Not like Egypt or Canaan: sexual boundaries
nodes.d: Leviticus 18 calls Israel not to follow the practices of Egypt or Canaan, listing forbidden sexual relations, Molech worship and other practices, and warns that the land vomits out nations that defile it.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why the chapter says the LORD is giving these commands, using what verses 3 and 24-30 say?
ev: Say whose ways Israel is told not to follow (18:3).
State the consequence the chapter gives for defiling the land (18:24-28).
Find 18:5 and say what it promises to the person who does the LORD's statutes.

nodes.t: "Ye shall be holy": laws for neighbours
nodes.d: Leviticus 19 gathers commands under the call to be holy because the LORD is holy: honouring parents, sabbaths, leaving gleanings for the poor, honest dealing, no partiality, loving one's neighbour as oneself, care for the stranger and just weights.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} list some ways Leviticus 19 says holiness shows up in daily life?
ev: Name at least five commands from the chapter that deal with how to treat other people.
Find the command to love the neighbour (19:18) and the command about the stranger (19:33-34).

nodes.t: Penalties for Molech worship, sorcery and sexual sin
nodes.d: Leviticus 20 repeats prohibitions on Molech worship, mediums, cursing parents and forbidden unions, attaching penalties to each, and ends by calling Israel to be holy and separate from the nations the LORD is casting out.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain how chapter 20 relates to the commands of chapters 18 and 19?
ev: Name three sins in the chapter and the penalty the text attaches to each.
Find what the LORD says in 20:26 about why Israel is to be holy.

nodes.d: Leviticus 21 lays down rules for the priests: limits on mourning, whom they may marry, higher standards for the high priest, and that a priest with a bodily blemish may eat the holy bread but may not approach the veil or altar.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why the text says the priests must be holy (21:6, 8)?
ev: Say how the high priest's rules differ from other priests' in 21:10-15.
State what a blemished priest may and may not do (21:21-23).

nodes.t: Eating the holy things and acceptable gifts
nodes.d: Leviticus 22 says who may and may not eat the holy offerings (uncleanness bars a priest; strangers and hired servants may not), and that offerings to the LORD must be without blemish.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why animals with defects were not acceptable as offerings?
ev: Name who may not eat of the holy things and what bars a priest from eating (22:3-9).
Say what the text says about offering blemished animals (22:20-25).

nodes.d: Leviticus 23:1-22 lists the weekly sabbath and the feasts of the LORD in spring and early summer: Passover and Unleavened Bread, the wave sheaf of firstfruits, and the feast of weeks fifty days later, with a reminder to leave the corners of the field for the poor.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} name the feasts in Leviticus 23:1-22 and when each was kept?
ev: Give the date and name of each feast in the first half of the chapter.
Say how the fifty days to the feast of weeks are counted (23:15-16).

nodes.d: Leviticus 23:23-44 sets out the feasts of the seventh month: the day of trumpets, the day of atonement with its affliction of souls, and the feast of tabernacles in which Israel dwells in booths so their generations remember the exodus.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the feast of tabernacles was meant to remind Israel of?
ev: Give the date of each feast in the seventh month.
Say why Israel was to live in booths (23:43).

nodes.t: The lamps and the bread of the presence
nodes.d: Leviticus 24:1-9 commands pure olive oil for the lamps to burn continually before the LORD and twelve cakes of fine flour set in two rows each sabbath on the table with frankincense, for Aaron and his sons to eat.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} describe the lamps and the twelve cakes in the tabernacle?
ev: Say what the lamps burn on and where the twelve cakes are set.
State who eats the cakes afterward.

nodes.t: The blasphemer and the law of equal justice
nodes.d: Leviticus 24:10-23 tells of a man, son of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian father, who blasphemed the name; the LORD tells Moses he is to be stoned, and gives the law of life for life, eye for eye, one law for stranger and native.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the law "eye for eye" (24:19-20) says is to be done, and who it applies to?
ev: Retell what the man did and what was decided.
Say what 24:22 says about the stranger and the native.

nodes.t: The sabbath year and the jubilee
nodes.d: Leviticus 25:1-22 commands a sabbath rest for the land every seventh year, and a jubilee after seven times seven years with trumpet, liberty and return to one's possession, with the LORD promising a blessing of enough produce in the sixth year.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the jubilee was and what it did for families and land?
ev: Describe what is not done to the land in the seventh year.
Say what happens in the fiftieth year (25:10-13) and how the LORD answers the question "what shall we eat?" (25:20-21).

nodes.d: Leviticus 25:23-55 teaches that the land is the LORD's and not to be sold permanently, provides for a kinsman to redeem land and a poor brother or sold person, forbids usury to a poor brother, and says Israel are the LORD's servants brought out of Egypt.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what a kinsman redeemer could do in Leviticus 25?
ev: Say who may redeem a poor man's land or person.
Find why the text says the land cannot be sold for ever (25:23) and why Israelites cannot be treated as slaves (25:42).

nodes.t: Blessings and curses of the covenant
nodes.d: Leviticus 26 sets before Israel blessings for walking in the statutes (rain, peace, God dwelling among them), and a graded series of punishments for disobedience ending in exile, with a promise to remember the covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham when they confess.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the chapter says will happen if Israel obeys, if Israel disobeys, and if Israel confesses?
ev: Summarise the blessings in 26:3-13 and the stages of discipline from 26:14 on.
Find the verses where the LORD promises to remember his covenant (26:42-45).

nodes.d: Leviticus 27 gives how a person, animal, house or field vowed to the LORD may be valued and redeemed (adding a fifth), what is devoted and cannot be redeemed, and that the tithe of land and herd is the LORD's.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what the text says about vows and the tithe?
ev: Say how a vowed field or house could be redeemed.
Name what the chapter says belongs to the LORD without being redeemed (27:26, 28, 30-33).

nodes.d: Genesis runs from creation (1:1) to the death of Joseph in Egypt (50:26): creation, the fall, the flood, Babel, and the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} outline Genesis in order, from creation to Joseph in Egypt?
ev: Name the four main sections: creation, fall and flood, Abraham, and the patriarchs through Joseph
Say where the story begins (1:1) and ends (50:26)

nodes.d: Numbers follows Israel from Sinai through the wilderness: the census, camp and Levites, departure from Sinai, the rebellion at Kadesh and forty years of wandering, Balaam, a second census, and preparation on the plains of Moab for entering the land.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} give a short summary of where Israel starts and ends in Numbers?
ev: Describe the journey in Numbers in three stages: at Sinai, wandering, and on the plains of Moab.

nodes.d: The gospel of Matthew, from the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David and son of Abraham (1:1), through the five great discourses, the passion and the resurrection, to the closing commission (28:16-20).
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain in a few sentences what Matthew is about and how it begins and ends?
ev: Describe the movement of the book: birth and preparation (1-4), the Sermon on the Mount (5-7), miracles and mission (8-12), parables of the kingdom (13), teaching on the way to Jerusalem (14-23), the coming kingdom (24-25), the passion and resurrection (26-28)
Name where the book starts and ends

nodes.t: Divorce, oaths, retaliation and love for enemies
nodes.d: Jesus teaches on divorce, on plain speech instead of oaths, on not resisting evil with evil, and on loving and praying for enemies, as the Father gives sun and rain to evil and good.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what Jesus says about loving enemies and why?
ev: Say what Jesus teaches about oaths (5:33-37)
Explain the command about enemies and the reason given in 5:45

nodes.t: The rich young man and rewards of following
nodes.d: A young man asks what good thing earns eternal life; told to keep the commandments and then to sell all and follow, he goes away sorrowful; Jesus speaks of the camel and needle and promises rewards to those who left all.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell what Jesus asked the young man to do and why it was hard?
ev: Say why the young man left sorrowful
Explain “with God all things are possible”

nodes.d: Asked which is the great commandment, Jesus answers love the Lord with all heart, soul and mind, and love your neighbour as yourself, and says all the law and the prophets hang on these two.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} say the two great commandments and what they cover?
ev: State the two commandments
Explain “on these two hang all the law and the prophets”

nodes.d: A scribe asks which commandment is first; Jesus answers the Lord is one and to love him with all heart, soul, mind and strength, and second to love your neighbour as yourself; the scribe agrees and Jesus says he is not far from the kingdom.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} say the two great commandments?
ev: State the two commandments
Say what the scribe added and what Jesus replied

nodes.d: Luke writes an orderly account for Theophilus so he may know the certainty of what he was taught, from the births of John and Jesus to the resurrection, ascension and the apostles' commission.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why Luke wrote his Gospel and where it begins and ends?
ev: Say who Luke addresses, why he wrote, and how the book begins and ends.

nodes.t: Simeon and Anna in the Temple
nodes.d: Jesus is named and presented at the temple; Simeon, to whom the Spirit promised he would see the Lord's Christ, blesses God for salvation for all peoples, and Anna the prophetess speaks of him to those awaiting redemption.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} say what Simeon and Anna said when they saw the child Jesus?
ev: Say what Simeon was waiting for and what he and Anna said.

nodes.d: Asked by a lawyer what he must do to inherit eternal life, Jesus draws out love of God and neighbour; to the question 'who is my neighbour' he tells of a Samaritan who helps a man left by robbers after a priest and a Levite pass by.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} retell the parable of the good Samaritan and say what Jesus told the lawyer to do?
ev: Retell the parable and say what Jesus told the lawyer to do.

nodes.d: Paul's letter to the Romans, from the greeting and the gospel theme (1:1-17) to its closing greetings and doxology (16:27).
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain in a few sentences what Romans is about, using 1:16-17?
ev: State the letter's theme from 1:16-17
Describe the movement: sin (1-3), justification (3-5), life in Christ and the Spirit (6-8), Israel (9-11), Christian living (12-16)

nodes.d: Righteousness is for everyone who believes; faith comes by hearing the word of Christ.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain Romans 10:9-10 and 10:17?
ev: State 10:9-10
Explain 10:17

nodes.d: Paul teaches submission to governing authorities as God's servants, and sums up the law in love for neighbour.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what Romans 13:1-7 teaches?
ev: State what Paul says about authorities (13:1-7)
Explain 13:8-10

nodes.d: Paul writes to the churches of Galatia, who were turning to another gospel, to defend justification by faith, the freedom of the sons of God and life by the Spirit (1:1-6:18).
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain why Paul wrote to the Galatians and what he says the true gospel is?
ev: Say what problem prompted the letter (1:6-9)
Name the three parts: Paul's defence (1-2), justification by faith (3-4), living by the Spirit (5-6)

nodes.t: Abraham, faith and the blessing for the nations
nodes.d: Paul argues that Abraham believed God and it was counted to him for righteousness, so those of faith are Abraham's children, and that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain how Galatians 3:6-9 connects Abraham's faith to the Gentiles?
ev: Quote what Paul says Abraham did (3:6)
Explain who are the children of Abraham (3:7)
Say what the scripture foresaw (3:8)
Explain how Christ redeemed us from the curse (3:13-14)

nodes.t: Walking by the Spirit: works of the flesh and fruit of the Spirit
nodes.d: Paul says freedom is for serving one another in love, that the whole law is fulfilled in loving your neighbour, and contrasts the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit for those who walk in the Spirit.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} name the fruit of the Spirit from Galatians 5:22-23 and explain the difference between flesh and Spirit?
ev: Say how liberty is to be used (5:13)
List some works of the flesh (5:19-21) and the fruit of the Spirit (5:22-23)
Say what belongs to those who are Christ's (5:24)

nodes.t: The first covenant's tabernacle and ordinances
nodes.d: The first covenant had a worldly sanctuary with a first tent and Most Holy Place containing the ark, and only the high priest entered once a year with blood; the writer says the Holy Spirit signified this could not perfect the conscience until a time of reformation.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} describe the tabernacle arrangements and what they could not do (9:1-10)?
ev: Name items in the Holiest of all (9:3-4)
Say what the Holy Spirit showed by the arrangement (9:8)

nodes.t: Leaders, Jesus outside the camp, and sacrifices of praise
nodes.d: Readers are to remember their leaders, avoid strange doctrines, go out to Jesus outside the camp bearing his reproach, seeking the city to come, and offer sacrifices of praise and doing good.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} explain what it means to go to Jesus outside the camp and what sacrifices God is pleased with (13:12-16)?
ev: Recite 13:8
Say where Jesus suffered and what believers are to do (13:12-13)
List the sacrifices of 13:15-16

nodes.d: James is a letter from James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes scattered abroad, with practical teaching on trials, living faith, the tongue, humility, wealth and patience.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} say what James tells believers to do with trials, words and wealth?
ev: Name the main themes of James in order
Say who the letter is from and to whom it is written

nodes.d: James rebukes giving the rich seats of honour and shaming the poor in the assembly, reminds them God chose the poor rich in faith, and calls loving your neighbour the royal law.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} tell what James says is wrong with favouring the rich over the poor?
ev: Describe the example of partiality in the assembly
Say what James calls the royal law
Explain why partiality is sin according to 2:9

nodes.t: Be holy: redeemed by precious blood
nodes.d: Peter calls believers to be holy as God is holy, reminds them they were redeemed by the precious blood of Christ the lamb without blemish, and says they were born again by the abiding word.
nodes.q: Can {{name}} say what Peter says paid the price for believers, and how they should live because of it?
ev: Say what Peter says redeemed them and what it was not
Explain the call to be holy in 1:15-16
Describe what the word of the Lord does according to 1:23-25
